chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: Which of these is an animal product?
solution: Honey is made by honeybees, so it is an animal product. Rice, spinach and mustard oil are plant products.

chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: Which plant part do we eat when we eat a carrot?
solution: A carrot is a modified tap root that stores food.

chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: Name three food items that come from plants and three that come from animals.
solution: Cereals, pulses, fruits and vegetables are plant foods; milk, egg, meat, fish and honey are animal foods.

chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: A cow is a ______.
solution: Cows eat grass and other plant material, so they are herbivores.

chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: Vultures that eat dead animals are best described as:
solution: Animals that feed on dead and decaying matter are scavengers.

chapter: Food: Where Does It Come From?
q: Why does a tiger have sharp, pointed teeth while a cow has flat teeth?
solution: Teeth are adapted to diet: tigers tear meat with pointed canines, cows grind plant material with flat molars.

q: Which nutrient is the main source of energy?
solution: Carbohydrates are the body's main fuel and are found in cereals, potato and sugar.

q: Iodine solution is used to test for:
solution: Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch.

q: Name the two groups of foods that protect the body from disease.
solution: Vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients; deficiency causes specific diseases.

q: Night blindness is caused by the deficiency of:
solution: Vitamin A is needed by the retina; carrots, papaya, mango and green leafy vegetables are good sources.

q: Goitre is caused by the deficiency of:
solution: Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones; iodised salt prevents goitre.

q: What is a balanced diet?
solution: It supplies energy, building material and protective nutrients in correct proportions, keeping the body healthy.

q: Jute fibre is obtained from the:
solution: Jute is a bast fibre taken from the stem of the plant.

q: The process of separating cotton fibres from seeds is called:
solution: Ginning separates seeds from cotton fibre.

q: Write the steps from fibre to fabric.
solution: Fibres are cleaned, spun into yarn on a spinning wheel or machine, then interlaced (woven) or looped (knitted) into fabric.

q: Which animal gives us wool?
solution: Sheep fleece is the most common source of wool.

q: Sericulture is the rearing of:
solution: Sericulture is silk farming.

q: Why is wool a good insulator?
solution: Air trapped between wool fibres is a poor conductor, so it reduces heat transfer from the body.

q: Which material is transparent?
solution: Glass allows most light to pass through.

q: Materials that do not allow electricity to pass are called:
solution: Insulators such as rubber and plastic resist the flow of current.

q: Name three properties used to sort materials.
solution: Appearance, hardness and solubility (also transparency and conductivity).

q: Why is the handle of a cooking pan made of plastic?
solution: Insulating handles stay cool enough to hold.
options: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat

q: Objects are grouped mainly to:
solution: Grouping reveals shared properties so materials can be used scientifically.

q: Give one example each of a soluble and an insoluble substance.
solution: Sugar dissolves in water, sand does not and settles at the bottom.

q: Winnowing separates components based on:
solution: Wind carries the lighter husk away while heavier grain falls close by.

q: Which method removes small stones from rice?
solution: Stones are visible and few, so they are removed by hand.

q: Why is threshing done before winnowing?
solution: You cannot blow away husk while it is still attached to the stalk.

q: The clear liquid that passes through filter paper is called:
solution: The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid left on the paper is the residue.

q: Which method recovers dissolved salt from salt water?
solution: Water evaporates and salt is left behind.

q: What is a saturated solution?
solution: Extra solute added to a saturated solution simply settles at the bottom.

q: Which of these changes is irreversible?
solution: Burning forms ash, smoke and gases — new substances that cannot be turned back into paper.

q: Melting of ice is a ______ change.
solution: Ice can be refrozen, so the change is reversible.

q: Give two examples each of reversible and irreversible changes.
solution: Reversible: melting of wax, dissolving salt. Irreversible: rusting of iron, cooking food.

topic: How Changes Happen: Heating, Cooling and Expansion
q: Most substances ______ on heating.
solution: Heating increases particle spacing, so solids and liquids expand.

topic: How Changes Happen: Heating, Cooling and Expansion
q: Gaps in railway tracks are left to allow for:
solution: Without gaps, expanding steel could buckle the track.

topic: How Changes Happen: Heating, Cooling and Expansion
q: Why does a metal lid open easily after being warmed?
solution: Differential expansion is used to open tightly stuck lids.

q: Carrot is an example of a:
solution: Carrot stores food in its tap root.

q: Water is transported through the plant by:
solution: Xylem carries water and minerals upward from the root.

q: State two functions of leaves.
solution: Leaves also lose water by transpiration, which helps pull water up the plant.

topic: Flowers, Fruits and the Basics of Photosynthesis
q: The female part of a flower is the:
solution: The pistil contains the stigma, style and ovary.

topic: Flowers, Fruits and the Basics of Photosynthesis
q: Which gas is released during photosynthesis?
solution: Oxygen is a by-product of splitting water during photosynthesis.

topic: Flowers, Fruits and the Basics of Photosynthesis
q: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
solution: The ovary becomes the fruit; ovules become seeds.

q: The elbow is an example of a:
solution: Elbows and knees work like door hinges.

q: Which structure protects the brain?
solution: The skull encloses the brain.

q: Why are joints needed?
solution: Different joint types permit different ranges of movement, from fixed skull plates to freely moving hips.

q: Muscles can only:
solution: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls; pairs of muscles produce opposite movements.

q: Earthworms move with the help of:
solution: Fluid pressure plus setae let the worm grip and extend its body.

q: Why do birds have hollow bones?
solution: Lightness reduces the energy needed to lift the body against gravity.

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
q: The camel's hump stores:
solution: The hump is a fat store that can be broken down for energy; it is not a water bag.

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
q: Gills help fish to:
solution: Gills absorb dissolved oxygen from water.

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
q: Define habitat.
solution: The place where an organism lives and obtains food, water, shelter and air.

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
topic: Acclimatisation and Life in Extreme Places
q: Acclimatisation is:
solution: It is a reversible, within-lifetime adjustment.
options: A short-term adjustment to the environment

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
topic: Acclimatisation and Life in Extreme Places
q: The percentage of Earth's surface covered by water is about:
solution: Water covers roughly 71% of the planet, and it makes up most of the living space.

chapter: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings
topic: Acclimatisation and Life in Extreme Places
q: Why do people living in mountains have more red blood cells?
solution: Thin air has less oxygen, so more red blood cells are needed to carry enough oxygen.

q: The SI unit of length is the:
solution: The metre is the SI base unit of length.

q: 1.5 m equals:
How would you measure the length of a curved line?
solution: Place a thread along the curve, mark the ends, straighten the thread and measure it with a scale.

q: The motion of a point on a fan blade is:
solution: A point on a rotating blade traces a circle.

q: A motion that repeats at equal intervals is called:
solution: Periodic motion returns to the same state again and again.

q: Give one example each of rectilinear and oscillatory motion.
solution: A car on a straight road (rectilinear) and a swinging pendulum (oscillatory).

q: A shadow is formed by:
solution: Only a light-blocking object produces a shadow.

q: In a pinhole camera the image is:
solution: Rays cross at the hole, so the image is inverted.

q: Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque: clear glass, butter paper, wood.
solution: Clear glass is transparent, butter paper is translucent and wood is opaque.

q: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
solution: The image cannot be caught on a screen and is upright.

q: A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror because it:
solution: A wider view shows more of the road behind.
options: Gives a wider field of view

q: Why does an ambulance carry 'AMBULANCE' written in reverse?
solution: So that drivers reading it in a mirror see it correctly, because a plane mirror laterally inverts the image.

topic: The Electric Cell and a Simple Circuit
q: Electric current flows in a circuit only when it is:
solution: A complete, closed path is needed.

topic: The Electric Cell and a Simple Circuit
q: Which of these is a conductor?
solution: Metals such as copper carry current.

topic: The Electric Cell and a Simple Circuit
q: How can you test whether a material is a conductor or insulator?
solution: Connect it in a simple circuit with a cell and bulb; if the bulb glows it is a conductor.

q: The symbol of a cell in a circuit diagram is:
solution: The long line is the positive terminal and the short line the negative terminal.
options: A long and a short parallel line

q: Water conducts electricity because it contains:
solution: Dissolved salts provide ions that carry charge.

q: Write two electric safety rules for home.
solution: Never touch switches with wet hands; never overload a socket or use damaged wires.

q: Which pair of poles attracts?
solution: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel.

q: Which of these is NOT attracted by a magnet?
solution: Copper is not a magnetic material.

q: How does a compass help in finding direction?
solution: Its magnetised needle aligns along Earth's magnetic field and points north–south.

q: An electromagnet loses its magnetism when:
solution: Magnetism depends on the flowing current.

q: To demagnetise a magnet you can:
solution: High temperature, hammering or dropping disturb the alignment of domains.

q: How should two bar magnets be stored?
solution: In pairs with opposite poles together and a soft iron piece across the ends.

q: The process of changing water vapour into liquid is:
solution: Cooling vapour forms droplets.

q: Water that collects underground is called:
solution: Water that seeps into the soil and fills the spaces above impermeable rock is groundwater.

q: List the steps of the water cycle.
solution: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection (runoff and groundwater).

q: Drip irrigation is useful because it:
solution: It minimises evaporation and runoff.
options: Delivers water directly to roots and saves water

q: Rainwater harvesting mainly helps to:
solution: Captured rain is stored or allowed to percolate into the ground.

q: Give three ways to save water at home.
solution: Fix leaks, turn off taps while brushing, reuse water for plants (also take shorter showers).

q: The gas present in the largest amount in air is:
solution: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere.

q: Which gas supports burning?
solution: Combustion needs oxygen.

q: Why does a burning candle go out when covered by a glass?
solution: The oxygen inside is used up, so combustion cannot continue.

topic: Life, Air and the Balance of Gases
q: During photosynthesis plants take in:
solution: Carbon dioxide is the carbon source for making food.

topic: Life, Air and the Balance of Gases
q: Air pollution can cause:
solution: Particles and gases irritate the lungs and worsen asthma.

topic: Life, Air and the Balance of Gases
q: How do plants help maintain the balance of gases in air?
solution: They take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis, balancing respiration.

q: Which waste is biodegradable?
solution: Peels are broken down by microorganisms.

q: Vermicomposting uses:
solution: Earthworms consume organic waste and produce nutrient-rich castings.

q: What is the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste? Give one example of each.
solution: Biodegradable waste is broken down by living organisms (peels); non-biodegradable waste is not (plastic).

q: The 3Rs of waste management are:
solution: These three strategies cut waste and conserve resources.

q: Recycling paper helps mainly by:
solution: Recycling reduces the need to cut trees and saves energy and water.

q: Give two ways you can reduce plastic use at home.
solution: Carry a cloth bag for shopping; refill bottles instead of buying new ones.
